newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan orders troubled bank to halt operations.
newsitem.headline: Japan orders troubled bank to halt operations.

text.p: Japanese authorities ordered a troubled bank to halt business on Thursday -- the first time they have done so in five decades -- and said the move was vital to help clean up the nation's bad loan mess.

Finance Ministry figures showed Hanwa Bank Ltd suffocating under a heap of 190 billion yen ($1.71 billion) in problem loans, against its comparatively puny capital of 20.3 billion yen ($182 million) at the end of September.

The ministry said it had suspended operations at the second-tier regional bank based in western Japan, except for withdrawals of deposits, because the bank could not recover its bad loans and was unable to operate as a going concern.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference, however, that the failure ought not to cause anxiety about Japan's financial system overall.

The ministry said depositors would be protected and that swift handling of banking failures was essential for the recovery of Japan's financial system -- a view echoed by Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita.

"The Bank of Japan believes that prompt measures to deal with insolvent financial institutions without delay will lead to the early rejuvenation of the functions of the Japanese financial system," he told a news conference.
Hanwa, employing about 900 people, operates mostly around the city of Osaka.

It was only the third bank failure in Japan since the end of World War Two. The two other failures, one last year and one this year, were handled by creating new banks to take over the failed institutions' business.
Eleven smaller credit unions and credit associations have also gone under since December 1994, analysts said.
Finance Ministry officials told a news conference that a new bank would also be set up in Hanwa's case, but simply for the purpose of winding up its business.
Hanwa, established in 1941, has book assets of about 658 billion yen ($5.92 billion). It is not one of Japan's top 20 commercial banks.
Like much of Japan's financial system, Hanwa was hard hit by the collapse of property prices from the sky-high levels of the 1980s "bubble" era, when share prices also soared.

Hanwa said on Thursday that it made a parent current loss of 33.72 billion yen ($303 million) in the six months to September 30. Two weeks ago, the bank forecast a loss of just 280 million yen ($2.52 million) for the period.
Current profit is pre-tax, including profits or losses from stock sales and other non-banking business.

Last year, Japan suffered its first bank failure since the war when Hyogo Bank, also based in western Japan, fell victim to bad loans. Another small regional bank went under earlier this year. In addition, 10 credit unions and one credit associations have failed since December 1994, analysts said.
Analysts welcomed the news as a sign that measures were in motion to clean up Japan's financial system problems, and markets took the news calmly.

Tokyo shares held steady, although some regional bank shares fell. The key Nikkei 225 average closed 0.22 percent lower at 21,143.34. Early gains in bond prices were offset by speculative selling, and Japanese government bonds ended lower.

The dollar was little affected in Tokyo trade, after news of Hanwa's failure helped limit its downside in New York on Wednesday. But the U.S. currency later edged up on talk that a major Japanese bank in New York might face problems.

An Asahi Bank spokesman told Reuters the bank was looking into a report by Kyodo news agency that its New York branch could face legal action for allegedly viewing a confidential Federal Reserve inspection report this summer.
Kyodo also quoted Asahi Bank's president, Shigehiko Yoshino, as saying the bank had not suffered any large losses. ($1=111 yen)
